https://www.politico.eu/article/ireland-.text: BRUSSELS — The Irish Council presidency welcomed “consensus” among governments to introduce new EU-wide levies on foreign polluters and electronic waste to finance the bloc’s next seven-year budget , according to a document seen by POLITICO. The EU’s 27 countries are narrowing down a list of potential new taxes, or own resources, to fund the bloc’s common cash pot as negotiations enter their crunch phase. Introducing new EU-wide levies is crucial to lay the groundwork for a budget agreement by the end of the year, before national elections in France, Spain and Italy in 2027 threaten to disrupt the negotiations. Advertisement Advertisement The president of the European Council, António Costa, urged national leaders to home in on several potential taxes during their next gathering in Brussels on Oct. 15. Supporters argue that own resources are essential to generate more revenue and reduce national contributions to the EU from 2028 to 2034. With less than four months to go until the informal deadline, the bloc's governments have shown openness towards a tax on foreign carbon imports, officially known as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and a separate levy on non-collected electronic waste. “Of the Commission’s proposals for new Own Resources, the most consensual among Member States is CBAM, with many open to increasing the call rate further,” the Irish Council presidency, which is steering discussions, wrote in a note to EU governments seen by POLITICO. Under current rules, capitals must funnel 75 percent of CBAM revenues to the EU budget, and retain 25 percent for their domestic budgets. CBAM is expected to generate, on average, €1.644 billion per year, roughly adding up to €11.5 billion for the whole budget cycle, according to an updated estimate by the European Commission seen by POLITICO. The Irish presidency also noted “a broad degree of support” among governments towards the electronic waste tax, which is expected to generate €17.9 billion per year. They added that criticism towards the levy largely focuses on statistical issues. Advertisement Advertisement More EU taxes France is leading the charge to introduce more EU taxes to generate extra revenue and further reduce national contributions to Brussels. Last year, the Commission proposed five new levies — targeting carbon imports, emissions trading scheme (ETS), non-collected electronic waste, corporate profits and tobacco products — worth €66 billion per year. But most of the ideas — which must be approved unanimously by EU members — have been met with resistance from national governments. António Costa arrives for a summit in Brussels on March 19, 2026. | Marco Tacca/Getty Images The Irish presidency noted that “a group of Member States remain opposed to ETS.” The group includes highly polluting Eastern countries, such as Poland and Hungary, who want to retain the ETS revenues for their domestic budgets. It also wrote that many governments criticized the tobacco tax and a majority opposed the corporate levy because it will undermine competitiveness. In a bid to break the deadlock, the European Parliament last spring proposed new levies on online gambling, crypto firms and digital giants. Advertisement Advertisement However, the Irish presidency threw cold water on these suggestions, noting that “most Member States were opposed to or doubted the ability for the EP proposals to be implemented by 2028.” They added that few countries showed openness toward the digital levy, but others warned against “geo-political concerns” such as the threat of retaliation by the U.S. Finally, Ireland noted that governments are divided around the idea of postponing repayments of the bloc's post-Covid recovery fund, which are expected to cost €25 billion per year.

Photograph: Abstract Aerial Art/Getty Images Schools England school inspections to be overhauled again after barrage of complaints Exclusive: Education secretary sends Ofsted back to ‘drawing board’ as teachers raise serious concerns about new system Kiran Stacey and Richard Adams Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.00 EDT Last modified on Fri 2 Oct 2026 12.19 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google School inspections in England will be overhauled for the second time in a year, after a barrage of complaints that the new system was dangerously stressful and damaging teachers’ mental health. Lucy Powell, the education secretary, will tell the schools regulator Ofsted to “go back to the drawing board” after becoming concerned that inspection changes overseen by her predecessor, Bridget Phillipson, were creating problems for headteachers. Sources say Powell does not want to scrap the new system of ratings, which score schools from “exceptional” to needing “urgent improvement” in six key areas, but she does want inspectors to take greater account of the social and economic background of each school and its pupils. New Ofsted inspection regime is damaging our health, headteachers say Read more Powell’s changes, which will be communicated to Ofsted in the coming weeks, will be the second set of major alterations to the school inspection regime in just over a year, after Labour’s election manifesto pledge to replace the previous inspection framework in the wake of the death of the headteacher Ruth Perry . One source said: “She wants Ofsted to go back to the drawing board when it comes to measuring inclusion in particular. That’s where most of the problems seem to lie.” Powell’s changes will mean a significant shift from those carried out by Phillipson, who is now equalities minister and party chair. The two MPs fought an occasionally bitter contest to become Labour’s deputy leader last year, during which allies of each traded insults and accusations. Andy Burnham promoted Powell, a long-term ally, to Phillipson’s job as education secretary when he entered Downing Street earlier this year. Powell told an event at last week’s Labour party conference: “I want to see a much stronger emphasis in the current inspection regime on context, much stronger than it is at the moment. “I think this is one of those areas that it’s not straightforward to sort of move the oil tanker around massively quickly, but we absolutely do need to see reforms there.” View image in fullscreen Lucy Powell on stage with Andy Burnham at the Labour party conference. Photograph: Victoria Jones/Shutterstock Ofsted declined to comment. The inspectorate has commissioned its own independent evaluation of the new framework, with an interim report due out later this year. Paul Whiteman, the general secretary of the National Association of Head Teachers, said he was encouraged that ministers were listening to the criticism of inspections being raised by parents and experts as well as teachers. Whiteman said: “We have serious concerns about fairness and comparability. Schools serve very different communities and face very different levels of challenge. Leaders working in areas of greater disadvantage, or with higher numbers of pupils with special educational needs (Send) and disabilities, must not be placed at a systemic disadvantage by an inspection framework that fails to properly reflect those contexts. “Inspection should take account of the circumstances in which schools are operating, while recognising the tremendous work many are doing to support children facing the greatest barriers. “There is a need for an inspection system that is rigorous and proportionate and which genuinely supports school improvement.” The new “report card” system came into force last year , replacing Ofsted’s headline inspection grades of “outstanding” to “inadequate”, with a more detailed system intended to put less pressure on schools. The new system was initially welcomed by teachers, though criticised by others who warned it would make it harder for parents to judge a school. Since its implementation however, the regime has been met with a flurry of complaints from school leaders, who say it is harming their mental health and creating greater stress than the system it replaced. Perry’s sister, Prof Julia Waters, said last month that she had been contacted by at least a dozen teachers left “feeling suicidal” by Ofsted inspections, and raised her concerns in a letter to the prime minister. Amanda Hulme, the headteacher of Claypool primary school in Bolton, told the Guardian last month that her most recent Ofsted inspection was the most stressful experience of her career. Unions have called for teachers to be given “urgent relief” from the new system, while some want Ofsted to stop grading their schools altogether. A survey of school staff inspected under the new regime found that two-thirds said it was as bad or worse than the framework it had replaced. The survey of National Education Union members also found that three out of four said the inspections had negatively affected their mental health, with one primary school teacher describing it as “a circle of stress and fear”. Ofsted drops ‘clumsy’ and ‘offensive’ guidance linking autism and extremism Read more Powell is understood to be concerned that schools in more “challenging” contexts are doing worse under the new system. A recent study by the former Ofsted inspector Steve Wren found schools with higher levels of children receiving free school meals (a key test of poverty) or Send support were receiving lower ratings than average. Wren also found that ratings for secondary schools were closely correlated with how well pupils had performed before they joined the school, suggesting inspectors were not taking sufficient account of previous attainment levels. Wren said in his analysis: “Do these grades represent the reality that secondary schools with lower prior attainment are doing a markedly worse job of educating their pupils, or is the framework biased against them, or are inspectors not skilled at spotting strengths in such contexts?” Explore more on these topics Schools Ofsted Lucy Powell Education policy Teachers' workload England news Share Reuse this content More on this story More on this story New Ofsted inspection regime is damaging our health, headteachers say Northern Ireland schools must give girls option to wear trousers from next year Ofsted drops ‘clumsy’ and ‘offensive’ guidance linking autism and extremism Mail on Sunday ends up funding state school scholarship via payout to MP Ofsted inspections pushing headteachers to ‘point of destruction’, union chief says England’s teenagers outperform peers in most countries in maths, reading and science Headteachers’ union considers strikes after judge rejects case against Ofsted ‘Our children are less cognitively capable,’ says neuroscientist who wants to cut screen use in schools Ofsted to press ahead with new inspection regime despite opposition Private schools offer 41% more tree shade than state schools in England Most viewed Most viewed Education Schools Teachers Universities Students
